project.name: treetracker-wallet-api
project.description: A Node.js/Express REST API for treetracker-wallet-api, a wallet service backed by PostgreSQL. It manages wallets, trust relationships between wallets, and token/bundle transfers (pending, fulfilled, declined, cancelled), using JWT (RS256) authentication and db-migrate for schema migrations.

tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: The README explains what treetracker-wallet-api is: a Node.js/Express REST API backed by PostgreSQL that manages wallets, trust relationships between wallets, and token/bundle transfers. It documents the layered service/model/repository architecture, JWT (RS256) authentication, schema validation, and the test suite, giving you the map for the rest of this tour.

tour.title: Bootstrap and App Configuration
tour.description: server.js is the process entry point: it loads environment variables, sets up logging, and starts the Express app listening on the configured port. app.js does the real assembly work: it enables CORS in dev, enforces content types, parses request bodies, mounts every route, and installs a global error handler. Together these two files are where the whole request/response pipeline is wired together.

tour.title: Routing Layer
tour.description: server/routes/index.js aggregates all Express sub-routers (auth, token, transfer, trust, wallet, event) into one array that app.js mounts. Each router, such as walletRouter.js, transferRouter.js, and trustRouter.js, maps a URL prefix (/wallets, /transfers, /trust_relationships) to its handler functions. This is the first stop for any incoming HTTP request, before it reaches business logic.

tour.title: Handlers and Request Validation
tour.description: Handlers sit directly behind the routers and are the last stop of the request lifecycle before business logic runs. Each handler validates its input with a Joi schema (schemas.js) and then delegates to the matching service: authHandler calls AuthService, transferHandler calls TransferService, trustHandler calls TrustService, and walletHandler calls WalletService and TrustService. Keeping validation and HTTP concerns here keeps the service layer free of Express-specific code.
tour.languageLesson: Joi schemas declaratively describe the shape of expected input. Validating at the handler boundary means services can trust their inputs are already well-formed, a common pattern for keeping business logic pure.

tour.title: Authentication: JWT and API Keys
tour.description: AuthService verifies a wallet's hashed password and, on success, calls JWTService to sign an RS256 JSON Web Token using key material from environment variables. Separately, ApiKeyService validates the TREETRACKER-API-KEY header on protected endpoints, checking for existence, deprecation, and endpoint-specific permissions like batch-create access. Every authenticated route in the routing layer from Step 3 passes through one or both of these checks.
tour.languageLesson: RS256 is an asymmetric JWT signing algorithm: a private key signs the token, and a separate public key verifies it. This lets other services verify tokens without ever having access to the signing secret.

tour.title: Service Layer: Business Logic
tour.description: Building on the handlers from Step 4, the service layer holds the real business rules. WalletService handles wallet CRUD, sub-wallet lookups, and control-over authorization checks. TrustService manages requesting, accepting, declining, and cancelling trust relationships between wallets. TransferService is the largest of the three: it orchestrates the full transfer lifecycle (initiate, accept, decline, cancel, fulfill), wrapping every operation in a database transaction and logging an event for each state change.

tour.title: Domain Models: Wallet, Trust, Transfer
tour.description: Beneath the services sit the domain models, which encode the core rules of the wallet/trust/transfer relationship. Wallet.js implements hierarchical control checks between parent and sub-wallets that both trust and transfer logic depend on. Trust.js manages the trust request/accept/decline lifecycle, and Transfer.js orchestrates trust checks, wallet-control checks, and state transitions (pending, requested, completed, cancelled) for every transfer. The enums in trust-enums.js and transfer-enum.js define the exact states and types these models move between.

tour.title: Repositories and Database Session
tour.description: Repositories are the data-access layer models rely on. BaseRepository provides shared CRUD, a recursive where-clause builder, pagination, and batch-insert logic reused by every entity repository, including WalletRepository's complex query that unions self, child, and managed wallets. All of this runs through Session.js, which wraps a knex connection to represent the current transaction, letting callers begin, commit, or roll back a transaction shared across multiple repository calls, exactly what TransferService from Step 6 relies on for atomic transfers.

tour.title: Database Schema and Migrations
tour.description: The db-migrate migrations define the PostgreSQL schema that the repositories from Step 8 query against. CreateTableWallet.js creates the core wallet table, CreateTableEntity-Trust.js creates the entity_trust table backing the Trust model, and CreateTableTransfer.js creates the transfer table with its state and type enum columns. The database README explains the db-migrate tool and command reference used to apply these migrations in order.
tour.languageLesson: Each db-migrate file pairs an up migration with a down migration, so schema changes are both forward-applicable and reversible. Migrations run in timestamp order, forming an append-only history of how the schema evolved.

tour.title: Testing Strategy: Unit, Integration, E2E
tour.description: The project layers three kinds of tests. Unit tests, like TransferService.spec.js, mock the Transfer, Token, Wallet, and Event dependencies to test business logic in isolation. Integration tests, like bundle-transfer-decline.spec.js, exercise real service and repository code against a database, seeded by seed.js, to verify a full scenario such as a declined transfer preserving the token count. End-to-end tests go further still, using config.js and bootstrap.js to run Mocha root hooks that seed and clear a live deployed environment through real HTTP calls, closest to what an actual API client experiences.

tour.title: Containerization
tour.description: The Dockerfile packages the application for deployment: a single-stage build based on node:16-alpine that installs dependencies with npm ci and starts the app with node. docker-compose.yml is used for local development, spinning up a PostgreSQL 13 database with fixed credentials and a named volume, so the app from Step 2 has a database to migrate and connect to without any manual setup.
tour.languageLesson: docker-compose.yml declares services, networks, and volumes as desired state. Named volumes persist data (like the database) across container restarts, while the compose file itself never appears in the production image.

tour.title: Kubernetes Deployment
tour.description: The Kustomize base manifests define how the containerized app from Step 11 runs in production. treetracker-wallet-api-deployment.yaml runs 2 replicas of the container, wiring in JWT keys, the database connection string, and AWS S3 credentials through Kubernetes secrets. kustomization.yaml aggregates the deployment, service, API gateway mapping, migration job, and RBAC manifests into a single applyable resource set, with environment-specific overlays layered on top for development, test, and production.
tour.languageLesson: Kubernetes Deployments manage rolling updates across pod replicas. Kustomize overlays let a shared base manifest be patched per environment without duplicating the whole YAML file, keeping dev, test, and production configuration in sync.

tour.title: CI/CD Pipelines
tour.description: GitHub Actions workflows tie the whole tour together. The pull-request workflow lints the code, runs the database migrations from Step 9 against a Postgres service container, and runs the test suite from Step 10 on every pull request. The push-to-master workflow chains three jobs: it builds and pushes a Docker image using the Dockerfile from Step 11, deploys it to the DigitalOcean Kubernetes dev cluster using the manifests from Step 12, and then runs end-to-end tests against the freshly deployed environment, closing the loop from code change to running service.
tour.languageLesson: GitHub Actions workflows use 'on' triggers to decide when they run, 'jobs' to define units of work that can run in parallel or be chained with 'needs', and 'steps' for sequential commands within a job.
